t: #3006 Find Beautiful Indices in the Given Array I
o: Index i is beautiful if s[i..i+|a|-1] equals a and some occurrence j of b satisfies |j - i| <= k. With |a|, |b| ≤ 10, finding all occurrences is cheap even by direct comparison; the real task is efficiently pairing each a-occurrence with a nearby b-occurrence. In example 1, 'my' occurs at 16 and 33, 'squirrel' at 4, 18 (and 25-ish region), and both 'my' hits have a squirrel hit within 15. In example 2, a = b = 'a' occurs at 0, and |0-0| ≤ 4, so [0] is returned.
k: Collect all occurrence positions of a and b into two sorted lists first.
For each a-occurrence i, we only need to know whether some b-occurrence lies in [i-k, i+k] — a nearest-neighbor query on a sorted list.
Binary search or a monotone two-pointer sweep answers that query in O(log n) or amortized O(1).

a.i: Find every occurrence of a and b (using the language's substring search; with pattern length ≤ 10 the total work is O(n·m) which is fine for n = 1e5). For each position i in the a-list, binary-search the b-list for the smallest j ≥ i-k and check j ≤ i+k.
s: Scan s collecting all start indices of a into list A and of b into list B.
For each i in A, binary search B for the first index ≥ i - k.
If that index exists and is ≤ i + k, append i to the answer (A is scanned in order, so output stays sorted).
a.t: O(n·m + |A| log |B|) — substring search costs O(n·m) with m ≤ 10, then one binary search per a-occurrence
a.sp: O(n) for the two occurrence lists

a.i: Since both lists are sorted and we process a-occurrences in increasing order, the pointer into B only moves forward: advance it past all b-occurrences smaller than i-k, then the current entry is the closest candidate on the left; check it against i+k. This removes the logarithmic factor.
s: Build occurrence lists A and B as in Approach 1.
Sweep i over A with pointer p into B, advancing while B[p] < i - k.
If p is in range and B[p] <= i + k, record i.
a.t: O(n·m + |A| + |B|) — linear sweeps dominate after the O(n·m) occurrence-finding phase

w: Either approach is fine here; mention KMP/Z-algorithm/rolling hash as the way to make occurrence-finding truly O(n) when patterns can be long (that is the Hard follow-up with |a|, |b| up to 1e5). Pitfalls: forgetting the answer must be sorted (scanning A in order handles it), boundary conditions i - k possibly negative, and overlapping occurrences (advance find by 1, not by the pattern length).
